new_statements.quote: The following are the rules for placing word stress or accent in QA: 1. Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is long. By a long syllable we mean any syllable which contains a long vowel, a consonant cluster or a geminate, e.g. /Xal'li:/ 'leave it!' /sa:'fart/ 'I travelled' /si'katt/ 'I became silent' 2. If the penult and the antepenult are short (by short syllable we mean any syllable which has a short vowel and zero or one arresting consonant) open syllables of the form CVCVCV(C), stress falls on the antepenult syllable, e.g. /'madalan/ 'for example' ... 3. Otherwise stress falls on the penult syllable, e.g. /'sikat/ 'he became silent' /mad'risi/ 'school' ... Stress has no phonological, morphological or syntactical function in Arabic.

Stress falls on the ult…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for gulf1241 (src qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to contradict; this work supplies an explicit weight-sensitive placement algorithm (heavy ultima, else antepenult in light CVCVCV(C), else penult) plus the statement that stress is non-contrastive. It is consistent with the summary of 'Bukshaisha 1985:8-9' that the earlier reading found second-hand in Shockley 2020, now verified against the original.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Predictable, quantity-sensitive stress in a three-syllable right-edge window: a heavy final syllable (long vowel, or closed by a cluster or geminate, i.e. CV: / CVCC; plain CVC does not count) takes stress; failing that, in CVCVCV(C) words with light open penult and antepenult stress is antepenultimate ('madalan); otherwise penultimate (mad'risi, tfa:'ragni, mustaffa'ja:tkum). Stress is stated to be non-contrastive ('no phonological, morphological or syntactical function'); the /'sikat/ ~ /si'katt/ alternation is explained as the suffix making the final syllable heavy. Instrumental chapter 6 adds that stress lengthens long vowels significantly but has no effect on short-vowel duration in QA (p. 464: 'Stress has a significant effect on the duration of long vowels only.. while it has no effect on the duration of short vowels.. This phenomenon seems to be particular to QA').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only a single primary stress is marked per word (examples up to seven syllables carry one stress mark).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. Related processes in sec. 1.1: elision of a short unstressed first-syllable vowel in disyllables (/ki'ta:b/ > /kta:b/), reduction of trisyllables (/'katabat/ > /'kitbat/), epenthesis into final obstruent+sonorant clusters (/2akl/ > /'2akil/) and a redundant prothetic vowel before initial clusters in citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Qatari Arabic (QA) as 'spoken by educated Qatari speakers in the capital, Doha'; data from the author and two other male speakers born and brought up in Doha (thesis ch. 3 intro, txt line ~507). This is the urban Doha variety within Gulf Arabic (gulf1241), not Bahraini, Kuwaiti or Emirati Gulf Arabic.

sources.quote: [p. 4] The two dialects have similar stress assignment rules, whereby stress is weight sensitive. Super-heavy syllables, CVVC/CVCC, attract stress, and if there are no super-heavy syllables, heavy syllables, CVV/CVC, receive stress. Typically, where there are two heavy syllables in the same word, for example, CVV.CVC, the heavy syllable with the long vowel, CVV, takes stress (see also Section 2.2). If two heavy syllables with similar structures occur in the same word, CVC.CVC, the penultimate receives stress. Unlike many other Arabic dialects (e.g., Egyptian or Levantine), Kuwaiti dialects, as well as some Gulf dialects, assign stress to the final heavy CVC in structures of the sequence CV.CVC (cf. Watson, 2011a, 2011b). [p. 5] 1.darb + na 'our road' 1.1. Hadari: ˈdarb.na 1.2. Bedouin: ˈdar.ba.na 2.beet + na 'our house' 2.1. Hadari: ˈbeet.na 2.2. Bedouin: ˈbee.ta.na [...] 3. xa.latˤ 'he mixed' 3.1. Hadari: xə.ˈlatˤ 3.2. Bedouin: xa.ˈlatˤ 4.ga.lab 'he overturned' 4.1. Hadari: gə.ˈlab 4.2. Bedouin: ga.ˈlab [p. 10, Table 1] ˈmar:at ˈba:sma ˈfa:tˤma [...] soˈbag naˈbe:l ʕaˈbi:r [...] ˈta:kil ˈbasma ˈbirħi [...] toˈbax ħaˈmad faˈgeʕ [...] ˈta:kil ˈmaryam ˈge:mar [...] kaˈlat beˈdo:r dʒ…

tone.quote: A relevant factor for the realisation of focus in EA is word stress, as stressed syllables have been characterised as the docking sites of pitch accents (Blodgett et al., 2007). According to Holes (1990), stress in EA is predictable, just as in other peninsular Arabic dialects. The stress assignment is determined based on (i) syllable weight, and (ii) syllable position of the word in question. In Arabic, there are three categories of syllable weight: superheavy (CVVC, CVCC), heavy (CVV, CVC), and light (CV). ... (9) Stress is on the superheavy syllable (if any), otherwise stress is on the penultimate syllable.
tone.locator: accepted-manuscript (page number 9), sec. 1.3 'Emirati Arabic'; the remark 'In EA, as a language without free word stress' is on MS p. 39
tone.summary: No lexical tone; f0 = intonation (focus, modality, boundary) over predictable weight-sensitive stress.

tone.quote: Based on our analyses, we propose an initial tonal inventory of two main pitch accents (i.e., H*, (LH)*), one downstepped variant (i.e., !H*), and four bitonal phrase accents (i.e., LL%, LH%, HL%, HH%), which mark the right edges of intonation phrases. The data suggest that speakers produce a pitch accent on every content word ... We represent pitch accents with asterisks that indicate a tonal target aligning with a syllable. (Lexical stress in Arabic is predictable, and pitch accents generally align with those stressed syllables.)
tone.locator: p. 1137, Abstract and sec. 2.1 'Corpus and approach'
tone.summary: No lexical tone; intonational pitch accents H*, (LH)*, !H* docking on predictable word stress; boundary tones LL% LH% HL% HH%.
